transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: Craig Reynolds's 1987 paper asks how a flock can move together without giving every bird a scripted path. Begin with separation. Each simulated agent steers away from close neighbors. Turn this rule off, reset the same seed, and compare the distance between agents over the next few seconds.

transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: Alignment matches the average velocity of nearby agents. It gradually coordinates their headings. Turn alignment off while leaving the other two rules on. The agents can still gather and avoid crowding, yet travel in less coordinated directions. Watch the order score change as those headings spread apart.

transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: Cohesion steers an agent toward the local center of its neighbors. It is different from alignment: location and heading are different information. It is also different from attraction toward one global center. Turn cohesion off and watch how the flock spreads. Resetting keeps the same initial conditions, making the comparison more useful.

transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: Select follow one agent. Its halo marks the distance limit, while the links identify neighbors within the forward-biased field of view. In this model that field spans two hundred and seventy degrees. Agents outside the neighborhood do not contribute to its three steering rules. Change the perception radius and observe how the local information changes.

transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: The group pattern emerges from repeated local decisions. Each agent steers using only its neighbors. Compare all three rules with a one-rule condition over several seconds. Look at the headings within each small group and compare them with the direction of the whole flock.

transcript.speaker: Clarity
transcript.dialogue: What happens when the flock meets an obstacle? In Reynolds's paper, the agent can give a turn to avoid the obstacle priority over flock centering. That allows the group to split around the obstacle. Once the way is clear, agents steer back toward their neighbors and the flock can regroup.
